symptoms: Small, dark brown to black circular lesions on leaves (often water-soaked initially).
Yellow halos frequently develop around leaf spots as they expand.
Severe infection leads to widespread blighting, yellowing, and defoliation.
Rough, scabby, raised circular lesions on green and ripening fruit.
causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas species.
Spread by wind-driven rain, splashing irrigation, contaminated seed, and handling wet plants.
Favored by warm temperatures (75°F–86°F / 24°C–30°C) and persistent leaf wetness or high humidity.
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds and disease-free transplants.
Employ drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers to minimize leaf wetness.
Practice crop rotation of at least 2–3 years with non-solanaceous crops.
Sanitize stakes, tools, and greenhouse benches between seasons.
management: Promptly rogue and destroy severely infected individual plants to reduce inoculum.
Avoid working in or harvesting fields when tomato foliage is wet.
Consult local agricultural extension agents for approved copper-based bactericides or biological control agents if disease pressure is high.
Apply organic mulch to reduce soil splash onto lower foliage.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension (EDIS PP-211)
Penn State Extension Plant Disease Factsheets

symptoms: Distinct concentric circular rings ('target board' appearance) on older, lower foliage.
Yellow chlorotic tissue surrounding expanding brown lesions.
Premature defoliation starting from the base of the canopy upwards.
Dark, sunken, leathery cankers at the stem base or fruit stem end.
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani.
Overwinters in infected crop debris, solanaceous weeds, and volunteer tomatoes.
Accelerated by warm temperatures (75°F–85°F / 24°C–29°C) accompanied by heavy dew or frequent rains.
prevention: Maintain wide plant spacing and staking to maximize airflow and sunlight penetration.
Prune bottom suckers and lower foliage (up to 12 inches off soil) to eliminate splash zones.
Rotate fields away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplants for 3 seasons.
Apply clean organic or plastic mulch around the plant base.
management: Strip and dispose of infected lower leaves at first sight; do not compost infected material.
Water strictly at the soil level using drip systems early in the morning.
Consult extension services regarding preventative bio-fungicides (e.g., Bacillus subtilis) or copper sprays before heavy humidity periods.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable MD Online
University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension (Early Blight on Tomato)

symptoms: Large, irregular, pale water-soaked lesions that rapidly turn dark brown to purplish-black.
White, velvety fungal-like downy growth visible on leaf undersides in high humidity.
Stems develop dark greasy-brown lesions; complete canopy collapse can occur within days.
Firm, greasy, golden-brown rot on green and mature fruits.
causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans.
High danger disease: highly infectious airborne sporangia travel miles on wind currents.
Favored by cool, humid, wet weather (60°F–70°F / 15°C–21°C) and persistent fog or rain.
prevention: Plant resistant cultivars (e.g., Mountain Magic, Defiant, Legend) where late blight is prevalent.
Destroy all volunteer tomato and potato cull piles before planting.
Monitor local university and agricultural late-blight forecast tracking networks.
Avoid overhead irrigation and ensure rapid foliage drying.
management: Late blight is a community-level threat; immediately report and destroy infected vines in sealed bags.
In commercial fields, harvest immediately if crop is mature or spray registered protectants in accordance with extension advice.
Do not leave infected vines in the field or uncovered compost heaps.
sources: USAblight Consortium
Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (Late Blight Fact Sheet)

symptoms: Pale greenish-yellow chlorotic spots with indistinct margins on upper leaf surfaces.
Olive-green to velvety brown mold growth directly underneath spots on leaf undersurface.
Infected leaves curl, wither, turn brown, and drop prematurely.
Primarily affects leaves, but blossoms and fruits may occasionally be infected.
causes: Fungus Passalora fulva.
Common in high tunnels, greenhouses, and humid, poorly ventilated outdoor plantings.
Thrives at high relative humidity (>85%) and warm temperatures (70°F–75°F / 21°C–24°C).
prevention: Maximize greenhouse ventilation with exhaust fans, roll-up sides, and circulating horizontal airflow fans.
Select leaf mold-resistant varieties featuring Cf-resistance genes.
Increase plant spacing to decrease humidity inside the canopy.
Water with subsurface drip irrigation to prevent surface evaporation.
management: Lower greenhouse humidity below 80% through night heating and morning venting.
Prune lower older leaves to enhance canopy airflow.
Sanitize greenhouse structure and equipment between cropping cycles with labeled disinfectants.
sources: University of Massachusetts Amherst Greenhouse Crops and Floriculture Program
Purdue University Extension (BP-197-W)

symptoms: Numerous small, circular lesions (1/16 to 1/8 inch) with dark brown borders and pale tan/gray centers.
Tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) clearly visible in lesion centers with a hand lens.
Severe leaf yellowing and shedding, beginning with the lowest foliage.
Fruit infection is rare, but defoliation exposes fruits to sunscald.
causes: Fungus Septoria lycopersici.
Overwinters in solanaceous crop residue and perennial weeds (e.g., horse nettle).
Disseminated by splashing rain, tools, insects, and handling wet plants.
Favored by wet conditions and moderate temperatures (68°F–77°F / 20°C–25°C).
prevention: Mulch heavily under plants immediately after transplanting to stop soil spores splashing.
Practice a minimum 2-year rotation with non-host crops (corn, beans, brassicas).
Weed control: eradicate nightshade and related weeds around garden perimeters.
Stake and trellis tomato plants to maintain upright, aerated growth.
management: Remove lower leaves showing early symptoms before spores spread upwards.
Avoid handling or cultivating tomato plants when moisture is on the leaves.
Apply organic copper or potassium bicarbonate according to agricultural extension guidelines.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Horticultural Guide
Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station (FS547)

symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling (pinpoint flecking) on upper leaf surfaces.
Silken webbing on leaf undersides, growing tips, and between stems.
Leaves turn bronze, dry out, become brittle, and drop as populations explode.
Stunted plant growth and sun-exposed, damaged fruit.
causes: Arachnid pest: Tetranychus urticae (Two-spotted spider mite).
Accelerates dramatically in hot, dry, dusty conditions (temperatures exceeding 85°F / 29°C).
Natural predators often wiped out by broad-spectrum synthetic insecticide use.
prevention: Keep garden paths watered or vegetated to suppress dust that inhibits mite predators.
Encourage native beneficial insects (ladybugs, lacewings, predatory mites Phytoseiulus persimilis).
Avoid over-fertilizing with high nitrogen, which encourages rapid pest reproduction.
Inspect leaf undersides regularly with a 10x hand lens during hot weather.
management: Wash foliage with a strong stream of water to dislodge mites and destroy webbing.
Apply insecticidal soaps or horticultural oils (e.g., neem oil) ensuring full coverage of leaf undersides.
Introduce commercial predatory mites in greenhouse or high tunnel settings.
Isolate and discard heavily infested foliage.
sources: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)
Colorado State University Extension Fact Sheet No. 5.507

symptoms: Pinpoint brown spots that expand into circular brown lesions with light brown centers.
Zonate concentric rings frequently develop inside lesions (resembling early blight).
Upper canopy leaves develop extensive chlorosis and drop.
Circular, deeply pitted, sunken lesions on fruit with dark centers.
causes: Fungal pathogen Corynespora cassiicola.
Broad host range infecting many vegetables and weeds.
Favored by warm temperatures (70°F–85°F / 21°C–29°C) and prolonged humidity or dew.
prevention: Promote canopy aeration with trellising and sucker pruning.
Avoid overhead irrigation, especially in late afternoon or evening.
Disinfect greenhouse stakes, wire supports, and equipment after harvest.
Rotate fields away from solanaceous and cucurbit crops.
management: Prune and safely destroy infected lower leaves.
Maintain balanced potassium and nitrogen nutrition to support plant vigor.
Consult extension agents for appropriate fungicide spray programs during severe outbreaks.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension (PP-237 Target Spot of Tomato)
North Carolina State University Extension Plant Pathology

symptoms: Marked upward curling and cupping of leaflets ('spooning').
Severe marginal and interveinal yellowing (chlorosis) of younger leaves.
Severe plant stunting and erect bushy appearance.
Flower buds drop prematurely; fruit set is drastically reduced if infected early.
causes: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus transmitted exclusively by the sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
Not transmitted through seeds or mechanical contact.
Prevalent in tropical, subtropical, and warm temperate tomato production areas.
prevention: Plant certified TYLCV-resistant or tolerant hybrids (e.g., Tycoon, Camaro, Charger).
Install fine insect netting (50-mesh) on greenhouse and nursery vents to exclude whiteflies.
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor and detect whitefly populations early.
Maintain a whitefly-free host-free period of at least 2 months between tomato crops.
management: Rogue and bag infected symptomatic plants immediately to prevent whiteflies spreading virus to neighbors.
Manage whitefly vectors with horticultural oils, insecticidal soaps, or biocontrols (Encarsia formosa).
Control alternate weed hosts (nightshades, mallows) surrounding the crop.
sources: UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl
University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension Service

symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves.
Distorted, curled, or fern-like ('shoestring') leaf shapes.
Stunted vegetative growth and reduced plant vigor.
Uneven ripening, internal browning, or yellowish-brown blotches on fruit.
causes: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV).
Extremely stable and persistent; easily transmitted mechanically by touch, pruning shears, and workers.
Can be seed-borne and survives in contaminated root debris and tobacco products.
prevention: Plant certified virus-free seeds and disease-resistant tomato varieties (labeled with 'T' or 'ToMV').
Instruct field workers to wash hands thoroughly with soap or 20% non-fat dry milk solution before handling plants.
Strictly prohibit smoking or handling tobacco products prior to handling tomato seedlings.
Sterilize cutting tools and pruning shears between plants using a 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) or bleach solution.
management: There is no chemical cure for viral infections; immediately remove and destroy infected plants.
Do not compost infected plants.
Clean and disinfect all stakes, pots, and soil trays.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension (Tomato Mosaic and Tobacco Mosaic Viruses)
Penn State Extension Plant Pathology Guidelines

symptoms: Foliage is vibrant, uniform green with normal leaf texture.
No chlorotic spots, wilting, mosaic mottling, necrotic lesions, or webbing detected.
Stems are sturdy and erect with consistent vegetative growth.
Flowers and fruits develop normally according to cultivar characteristics.
causes: Optimal cultural care, balanced soil nutrition, and absence of significant pathogen pressure.
prevention: Continue consistent watering at soil level (approx. 1–2 inches per week depending on weather).
Maintain proper soil pH (6.2–6.8) and supply balanced N-P-K with essential micronutrients (calcium, magnesium).
Keep mulch layer intact to regulate soil temperature and conserve moisture.
Perform regular scouting every 2–3 days for early identification of pests or disease.
management: Support growing vines with stakes, cages, or trellis systems.
Prune indeterminate varieties for adequate aeration and light penetration.
Harvest ripe fruit promptly to reduce physical stress on the vine.
sources: University of California Division of Agriculture and Natural Resources (UC ANR)
Penn State Extension Commercial Tomato Production Guide
